title: Lucent Android handheld device-profile dataset
purpose: Per-device screen geometry, physical control inventory and Android input-reporting behaviour, plus a small set of shared layout classes, so Lucent can size its game list, box art and preview video correctly and can name on-screen button hints by the label physically printed on the device in the user's hands.

conventions.unverifiedRule: Any scalar that could not be confirmed from a real source carries the exact string "UNVERIFIED" instead of a guessed value. Every such path is ALSO listed in that device's `unverified` array, so a consumer can find the gaps without walking the whole object. Absence of a key means the concept does not apply to that device (e.g. `screens[1]` on a single-screen handheld); it never means "unknown".
conventions.conflictRule: Where two credible sources disagree, the field is set to "UNVERIFIED" and the disagreement is recorded in that device's `conflicts` array with both claims and both URLs. A conflict is never silently resolved in favour of the more convenient value.
conventions.positionalSlots: Face buttons are recorded by PHYSICAL POSITION (north = top, south = bottom, east = right, west = left) mapped to the LABEL SILKSCREENED at that position. This matches Lucent's CanonicalControl enum (NORTH/SOUTH/EAST/WEST) in unified-android/src/com/thorium/lucent/input/CanonicalControl.java. The legend renderer must look up the label by slot; it must never hard-code a letter.
conventions.aspectDecimals: aspectRatio.decimal is width/height IN THE ORIENTATION THE SCREEN IS ACTUALLY USED, rounded to 4 significant places. Panels whose native scan orientation is portrait but which are used in landscape record both `nativeResolution` and `usedResolution`.

sourceKinds.on-device: Measured by the Lucent team on physical hardware. Highest confidence.
sourceKinds.primary-code: Read out of source that runs on the device or drives it: AOSP key layouts, RetroArch/libretro autoconfig, SDL_GameControllerDB, Unreal Engine's Android input table, vendor firmware/driver source.
sourceKinds.manufacturer: Vendor spec page, official store listing, or official manual PDF.
sourceKinds.review: Named hands-on review by a reputable outlet.
sourceKinds.database: Community spec aggregator. Lowest confidence; several are demonstrably wrong on control details and are only used where nothing better exists.

schemaNotes: Six-button face clusters (Sega Saturn style) do not fit the four-slot diamond. Those devices set controls.faceButtons.arrangement to "sega-six-arc" and populate `slots` with the LOWER arc plus `upperArcSlots` with the upper arc. Lucent's SystemControlLayouts currently routes Sega six-button games through L1/NORTH/R1 on a four-button device; on a real six-button device that remap is wrong and must be bypassed. This is a known assumption-breaker.

Devices with a trackpad standing in for a second stick (AYANEO Pocket DMG) or with a slidepad instead of a thumbstick (Retroid Pocket 2, Retroid Pocket Flip) report sticks.count for real thumbsticks only and describe the substitute in controls.alternateAnalog. A consumer that reads sticks.count alone will under-count the device's analog capability.

Phone-clamp controllers have no display of their own. They carry `hostDisplay: true`, an empty `screens` array, and a `layoutClassId` chosen from the HOST PHONE's runtime geometry, not from any baked-in panel. Their `layoutClassId` is advisory only: the app must query real window metrics at runtime.

Several devices expose a user-selectable trigger reporting mode (digital / analog / both) and a user-selectable face-button style (Nintendo / Xbox). On those devices the reported keycodes are NOT a fixed property of the hardware. triggerReporting.userSelectableMode and controls.faceButtons.softwareSwappable flag this; a profile keyed only on VID/PID will be wrong for one of the modes. On the Retroid Pocket 5 and the original AYN Odin the mode change alters the USB product ID itself.

AYANEO Pocket VERT and Retroid Pocket Classic have no analog sticks at all; Anbernic RG Rotate and AYANEO Pocket Micro Classic likewise. Any layout that requires a right stick to reach a view must degrade per the layout class's gracefulDegradation block.

boxArtNominalAspects.note: These are art-convention defaults for sizing a frame, NOT device facts, and are not marked UNVERIFIED because they are a Lucent editorial choice rather than a claim about hardware. Real scraped artwork varies per title and per region; the layout rule below is what actually guarantees nothing crops.
boxArtNominalAspects.rule: Fit-to-CONTAIN inside a frame whose HEIGHT is fixed by the layout class. Width is whatever the individual image's ratio yields, centred, with the slack absorbed by the surrounding pane. Never fix the width first, never crop to fill, never upscale past 1.0 device-pixel-per-source-pixel.

controlTiers.description: Two clickable thumbsticks (L3/R3), D-pad, four face buttons, four shoulders. The Lucent reference inventory.
Two thumbsticks but the sticks do not click, so L3/R3 do not exist.
One thumbstick, or one thumbstick plus a non-stick analog substitute (slidepad, trackpad). No usable right stick.
No analog sticks at all. D-pad only. No L3/R3.
Six face buttons in two arcs (Sega Saturn style). May or may not have sticks; check controls.sticks.

layoutClasses.rationale: Horizontal room is abundant and vertical room is scarce. Anything sized off screen WIDTH here becomes absurdly large; everything must be height-driven. This is the phone-clamp case and the only class where a five-hint legend comfortably fits on one row.

boxArt.scalingNote: At 21:9 a 3:4 box occupies only about 20% of screen width at 62% height, which is correct — let the detail pane keep the slack rather than growing the art. Wider art (DVD/arcade at ~0.71) simply gets wider at the same height, so the row never reflows.

previewVideo.note: Preview media that is not 16:9 (4:3 arcade captures, 3:2 handheld captures) pillarboxes inside the fixed frame. Never stretch to fill: an ultrawide screen makes horizontal stretch extremely visible.

layoutClasses.rationale: The most common bucket and the design reference. Side-by-side list and detail both fit without compromise.

boxArt.scalingNote: 3:4 art at 55% height uses about 23% of a 16:9 screen's width, leaving the detail pane room for the video beside it. At 5:3 and 16:10 the same fraction yields slightly wider art relative to the pane, which is fine — the pane, not the art, absorbs it.

layoutClasses.rationale: Noticeably squarer than 16:9. A 68% detail pane stops being wide enough to hold portrait art and a video side by side at comfortable sizes, so the detail pane stacks instead of splitting.

boxArt.scalingNote: Art sits above the video rather than beside it. Dropping the height fraction to 0.50 leaves room for a 16:9 video strip underneath without either element shrinking below legibility.

layoutClasses.rationale: Portrait box art and a 4:3 screen are close in proportion, so art wants to dominate. The detail pane must stack (art over video) or the video ends up postage-stamp sized. Several devices in this bucket are also low-resolution (640x480), so the legend must be allowed to wrap.

boxArt.scalingNote: On a 4:3 screen a 3:4 box at 48% height uses about 48% of the detail pane's width. Wide art families (DVD 0.71, arcade 0.71) reach about 51% at the same height. Both fit; neither crops.

previewVideo.note: The frame is 4:3 rather than 16:9 here because most preview media for the systems these devices actually run is 4:3 or narrower, and a 16:9 frame on a 4:3 screen wastes vertical space that this bucket does not have.

layoutClasses.rationale: The hardest bucket. There is not enough horizontal room for two panes, so split-pane is abandoned entirely: the list is full-width and the detail view is a separate pushed view. Portrait box art is the ONE thing that fits this shape naturally, so it leads.

boxArt.scalingNote: On a 1:1 screen a 3:4 box at 52% height uses 39% of the width — comfortably centred with metadata either side. Do not raise this to fill the width: a 0.71 DVD-case image at 52% height already reaches 37%, and pushing to width-fit would crop the taller cartridge art.

previewVideo.note: Do not impose a frame here. A 16:9 clip on a 1:1 screen occupies 56% of the screen height at full width; that is the correct result and reserving a taller fixed frame would leave a dead band. Reserve exactly the height the media needs.

layoutClasses.rationale: Vertical form factors where the panel itself is portrait. Everything is a single column; there is no detail pane at all, only a pushed detail view.

boxArt.scalingNote: This is the ONLY class sized by width rather than height, because on a portrait screen height is the abundant axis. A 3:4 box at 70% width uses 93% of the width's worth of height, which on a 0.75-aspect screen is about 70% of screen height — acceptable because the detail view is a dedicated screen.

layoutClasses.displayName: Two screens, wide primary plus a companion secondary
layoutClasses.rationale: The AYN Thor case, and the reason this dataset exists. The primary behaves exactly like single-wide, but the secondary screen absorbs one whole responsibility so the primary can breathe. WHICH responsibility depends on the secondary's aspect, which differs sharply between devices in this class (Thor 1.1481, AYANEO Pocket DS 1.3333).

primaryScreen.note: One extra grid column versus single-wide, because the secondary screen has taken either the video or the art off the primary.

secondaryScreen.selectionRule: If secondaryAspectDecimal >= 1.55, the secondary hosts the PREVIEW VIDEO full-bleed (contain, centred, black surround) and the primary detail pane gives its video slot back to the box art. If secondaryAspectDecimal < 1.55, the secondary hosts LARGE BOX ART plus metadata and the preview video stays on the primary. Rationale: a 16:9 clip on a 1.1481 panel wastes 35% of that panel to letterboxing, whereas portrait box art on a near-square panel is close to ideal.
secondaryScreen.touchRule: If the secondary screen reports touch, it is also the direct-manipulation surface: tapping the art or the video launches. If it does not, the secondary is display-only and must never be the sole route to any action.
secondaryScreen.presentationFlagNote: A secondary display carrying FLAG_PRESENTATION must be driven through a Presentation, not by resizing the main window across both panels.

legend.secondaryScreenLegend: none, except a one-line caption naming the button that swaps which screen has focus, if the device has such a button

layoutClasses.rationale: Anbernic RG DS: two identical 4:3 640x480 panels, both touch. Neither panel is big enough or wide enough to run a split pane, and they are equal, so responsibilities split cleanly one per screen rather than one screen serving the other.

primaryScreen.note: The lower/touch panel is the list, because it is the one under the user's thumbs.

layoutClasses.lowResolutionRule: At 640x480 per panel, minimum legible glyph height is the binding constraint, not proportion. Cap the list at 6 visible rows and drop metadata fields from the tail of the list before shrinking type.

legendModel.principle: A legend hint NEVER contains a hard-coded letter. It contains an ACTION and a positional SLOT. The renderer resolves the slot against the device profile's controls.faceButtons.slots (or shoulders.labels / systemButtons) to get the string physically printed on that device. On a Nintendo-layout device the confirm hint therefore points at the EAST button; on an Xbox-layout device the same hint points at SOUTH. Both render the text "A" because both devices print "A" on the button the user should press — which is the entire point.

xbox.note: Android's own convention. KEYCODE_BUTTON_A is the bottom button.

nintendo.note: The bottom button is printed B. Confirming on SOUTH here would tell the user to press B to launch a game.

playstation.note: Modern PlayStation convention: Cross confirms, Circle backs out. Regional Japanese titles historically inverted this; Lucent's own frontend does not.

sega6.note: Lower arc reads A-B-C left to right, so SOUTH is B and WEST is A. Confirm on the middle button, back on the left, matching Saturn menu convention.

unlabelled.note: Device ships blank caps. Legend must fall back to a rendered glyph of the button's POSITION (a small diamond with one pip filled), never a letter.

unknown.note: Used only where the silkscreen could not be verified. Legend must render the positional glyph, not a letter, until the device is confirmed. Rendering a letter we are not sure of is worse than rendering no letter.

noRightStick.layout: No layout change. Any view reachable only by the right stick must gain a second route before this device is shipped to; Lucent's RightStickViewRouter is the code path to check.

noAnalogSticks.layout: D-pad becomes the sole navigation device. Increase list row height by 15% and disable any momentum/inertial scrolling, because a D-pad produces discrete steps and inertial overshoot is disorienting without an analog axis.

twoFaceButtonsOnly.layout: Legend collapses to confirm, back and menu. No device in this dataset currently hits this case; it exists so the renderer degrades rather than rendering an empty slot.

sixFaceButtons.layout: Legend may use 4 hints on the face cluster instead of 3, since the extra arc is genuinely there. Do NOT route Sega six-button emulation through L1/R1 on these devices.

noTouch.applies: screens[].touch == false on the screen in question
noTouch.layout: Every action must be reachable by button. A non-touch secondary screen is display-only and must not carry the sole affordance for anything.
noTouch.note: No handheld in this dataset has a non-touch PRIMARY screen except the Retroid Pocket 2 (640x480, no touchscreen).

unknownFaceLabels.layout: Render positional glyphs instead of letters for every face hint on that device. Never substitute a plausible letter.
unknownFaceLabels.rationale: A wrong letter is actively harmful: it teaches the user to press the wrong button and looks like a bug in the emulator rather than in the profile.

triggerReporting.note: Confirmed by the Lucent team on physical hardware: the analog triggers arrive as MotionEvent AXES, and KEYCODE_BUTTON_L2 / KEYCODE_BUTTON_R2 do nothing. Which of the two axis pairs carries them (AXIS_LTRIGGER/AXIS_RTRIGGER versus AXIS_BRAKE/AXIS_GAS) has not been pinned down; Lucent's InputRouter accepts either pair, which is why it works without the distinction being recorded.

triggerReporting.note: THE MOST DANGEROUS ENTRY IN THIS DATASET. Unreal Engine's Android input code branches on API level for this exact device. On Android 12+ (API >= 31) triggers arrive on AXIS_LTRIGGER / AXIS_RTRIGGER. On PRE-Android-12 the engine sets bMapZRZToTriggers, so triggers arrive on AXIS_Z / AXIS_RZ RESTING AT -1.0 and travelling to +1.0, AND THE RIGHT STICK MOVES TO AXIS_RX / AXIS_RY. Lucent's DeviceCatalog maps the right stick to AXIS_Z / AXIS_RZ, so on a pre-Android-12 host this device would drive the camera with its triggers. No discrete L2/R2 keycode is delivered in either case.

androidAxisReference.note: Recorded here because it is the key that makes every triggerReporting field in this dataset readable, and because two incompatible conventions are BOTH in live use. Verified from AOSP's MotionEvent.java and from RetroArch's android_input.c.
androidAxisReference.libretroAutoconfigDecoder: In any libretro android/*.cfg: input_l2_axis="+6"/"+7" means AXIS_LTRIGGER/AXIS_RTRIGGER; "+8"/"+9" means AXIS_BRAKE/AXIS_GAS. input_l2_btn="104" means KEYCODE_BUTTON_L2. RetroArch's android_input.c writes analog_state[6]=ltrig, [7]=rtrig, [8]=brake, [9]=gas.
androidAxisReference.sdlDecoder: In SDL_GameControllerDB: lefttrigger:aN means an AXIS; lefttrigger:bN means a digital BUTTON. Do NOT read VID/PID from every platform:Android row — SDL falls back to a hash of the device descriptor string when real IDs are unavailable, and those GUIDs decode to ASCII garbage. Decode chars 8-11 as VID and 16-19 as PID little-endian, then sanity-check the VID against a known vendor.
androidAxisReference.aospGenericKl: Devices with no vendor-specific key layout inherit AOSP's Generic.kl, which maps ABS_GAS to AXIS_RTRIGGER, ABS_BRAKE to AXIS_LTRIGGER, and BTN_TL2/BTN_TR2 to keycodes 104/105 — but maps ABS_Z/ABS_RZ to the RIGHT STICK. A pad using the xpad ABS_Z/ABS_RZ trigger convention will therefore have its triggers masquerade as the right stick. This is the single biggest correctness trap in Android gamepad handling and it is why Lucent's InputRouter accepts both AXIS_LTRIGGER/AXIS_BRAKE for L2 and both AXIS_RTRIGGER/AXIS_GAS for R2.
androidAxisReference.swapWarning: L/R index swaps are common in community-contributed mappings. Several devices in this dataset have two rows with left and right reversed. A profile format needs an explicit per-device axis-source field and a swap flag; one convention cannot be assumed.
